prompt: ty rejects a valid program that uses a settings class from the pydantic-settings package. The user sets an environment variable, then defines a class that inherits from the settings base class of pydantic-settings, with one required string field whose name matches the environment variable. The program creates an instance of the class with no arguments and prints the field. At runtime this works and prints the value from the environment. ty flags the call with no arguments as an error, because it treats the field as a value that the caller must pass. mypy without the pydantic plugin reports a similar error, and mypy with the pydantic plugin reports no issue, because the plugin knows that the fields of such a settings class can be filled from environment variables. ty should also know this and not demand the field values in the constructor call of a pydantic-settings class. Seen with ty 0.0.1-alpha.19.
ty demands every field when I construct a pydantic-settings settings class, but those values can come from environment variables. Please stop requiring them, like mypy's pydantic plugin does.

ty gives a false error when a pydantic model gets fields from a mixin class. The user defines a plain mixin class, which does not inherit from the pydantic base model, with one annotated boolean field that uses pydantic's field function. Then they define a model that inherits from the pydantic base model and from the mixin, with one more annotated boolean field of its own. They create the model with keyword arguments for both fields and print the dumped model. At runtime this works and the output contains both fields, the mixin field first. ty instead reports an error on the keyword argument for the mixin's field, as if the model had no such parameter. ty should treat annotated fields that come from such a mixin as fields of the model, so the constructor accepts them. Seen with ty 0.0.54.
ty rejects constructor keyword arguments for fields declared on a plain mixin class that a pydantic model also inherits from. Those fields should be accepted.

In ty 0.0.57, when a pydantic model field is annotated with pydantic's JSON value type, the type that ty infers for that parameter of the model constructor in the default, non-strict validation mode is too wide. It contains plain Any at the top level, plus any iterable and any mapping with string keys. But pydantic rejects arbitrary top-level objects, iterables and mappings for this field type. So ty accepts calls that fail at runtime: a bytes value, a plain object instance, the Ellipsis value, a tuple, or a dictionary-like object from the collections module that is not a real dict. Calls that work at runtime must stay accepted: a list of numbers, a dict with string keys, and a dict with bytes keys (pydantic turns the key into a string). The constructor parameter type should keep the JSON shape: a list, a dict with string or bytes keys, a string, a bool, an int, a float, or None. The exact display can differ. The nested positions inside lists and dicts may stay loosely checked; that is not the same as Any at the top level.
For a pydantic field typed as pydantic's JSON value type, ty's constructor accepts any object. Allow only JSON-shaped values at the top level; nested contents may stay loosely checked.

ty repeats one correct error several times for an overloaded TypeIs function. The user writes a function with two overloads and an implementation. The first overload takes a parameter of type Never and returns TypeIs of bool. The second overload takes an object and returns TypeIs of str. The implementation takes an object and returns bool. The first overload is wrong, because bool is not compatible with Never as the type of the checked parameter. ty reports this error three times with the same text: once at the return type of the first overload, once at the return type of the second overload, and once at the return type of the implementation. The error is correct, but it should appear only once. The case comes up in practice with the standard library function that tells whether a value is a dataclass, as typeshed declares it. Seen with ty 0.0.58.
ty reports the same TypeIs error on every overload and the implementation when only one overload is wrong. Report it only once.

ty check becomes very slow and does not finish within five seconds on a small file. The file defines 21 typed dicts with the functional syntax, each with total set to false and one key "tag" whose type is a different string literal for each typed dict. A type alias is the union of the 21 typed dicts and str. A function takes a parameter of that union type. If an isinstance check shows that the value is a dict, the function passes the value to the dict() constructor. There is no ty configuration. Any one of these changes makes ty finish at once: remove the isinstance check; remove str from the union and pass the union of typed dicts directly to dict(); use the copy method or dict unpacking instead of dict(); or give all variants the same tag type str, so they are structurally the same. So the slow case needs a wide union of structurally different typed dicts, the isinstance narrowing to dict, and the call of dict() with the narrowed union. An earlier speed-up for a union made only of typed dicts passed to dict() does not seem to apply to the narrowed union. Type checking should finish in a reasonable time. Seen with ty 0.0.58 on Linux.
ty hangs when a wide union of TypedDicts plus str is narrowed by an isinstance check against dict and then passed to dict(). Make it finish quickly.

Ruff has a lint rule, still in preview, that warns when a class inherits from dict, list or str. The rule currently also reports such classes in stub files (.pyi). It should not apply to stubs. Stub authors should match the runtime code faithfully, so if the runtime class inherits from dict, list or str, the stub must do the same. Authors of third-party stubs cannot change the runtime code, and for first-party stubs the rule already reports the class in its .py source file. Seen with Ruff 0.8.5.
Ruff's preview rule that warns about classes inheriting from dict, list or str also fires in .pyi stub files. Stop reporting it in stubs.

Feature request for ty: narrow a value when it is checked with in against a list or a set that is written inline and holds only literals. Take a parameter whose type is a union of the string literals "A", "B" and "C". If the code checks whether the value is in a tuple of "A" and "B", ty narrows correctly: in the else branch the value is the literal "C". If the code checks the same membership with an inline list or an inline set of "A" and "B", ty does not narrow, and the else branch still shows all three literals. Because of this, the user cannot exhaust the literals and end with an assert_never call. The workarounds are to compare the value with each element using == and or, or to use a tuple, but many people use lists, and some use sets. The mutability of a list is not needed for such a check. So for such a check, where all elements are literals, ty should treat the list or set like the tuple and narrow the value the same way, in the true branch and in the else branch. Pyright does not do this either.
Make "x in [a, b]" and "x in {a, b}" with literal elements narrow x the same way the tuple form does, in both the true and else branches.

ty treats attribute writes through a metaclass differently from the other cases. If a class defines the special method that Python calls when an attribute is assigned, ty accepts writes of undeclared attributes on its instances. If a metaclass defines the special methods for attribute reads and attribute writes, ty accepts reads of an undeclared attribute from a class that uses it. But a write of an undeclared attribute on such a class gives a false error that the attribute does not exist on the class type. mypy accepts all three.

Reproduction with ty 0.0.51 and Python 3.10: a metaclass derived from type defines a read method that returns an int, and a write method that takes the attribute name as a string and the value as an int. A class uses this metaclass and declares nothing. In a function whose parameter is annotated as the type of that class, a read of any attribute of the parameter is accepted, but an assignment of 5 to that attribute is reported as an error. The error is only on the write.

Real case: a schema library whose metaclass defines both methods, so users add a property to a schema class by assignment. Reads check cleanly, but every such assignment needs a suppression comment.

Expected: ty uses the metaclass's write method for writes of undeclared class attributes, the same way it uses an instance-level write method for instance attributes.
ty gives a false error when I set a new attribute on a class whose metaclass defines its own attribute-setting method. Check such writes through that method, as for instances.

ty infers a strange type for a constructor call when the class's instance-creation method is wrongly decorated as a class method. That method should always be a static method. Example: a class defines the instance-creation method, decorated as a class method, that takes only the class argument and is annotated to return the typing Self type. Its body creates a plain object of the class, sets an attribute on it and returns it. Then the class is called with no arguments and the type of the result is revealed. ty correctly reports an error for the call, because the call fails at runtime. But it reveals the class object itself as the type of the result. All other type checkers infer an instance of the class. Expected: ty keeps the error and infers an instance of the class as the result of the call.
When a class's instance-creation method is wrongly decorated as a classmethod and returns Self, ty types the constructor call as the class object instead of an instance. Please fix.

A generic protocol that means "exactly this type, not a subtype" does not work in ty when the type argument is float. The protocol has one type variable. It declares the object's class attribute as a read and write property whose getter returns and whose setter takes the type object of that type variable. The pattern comes from a Python forum thread about overloads for bool versus int. It excludes bool from int, and bool and int from float. With float as the type argument it works with mypy, pyright and pyrefly, but not with ty.

Example: a timestamp class has a multiplication method whose other operand is annotated as this protocol with float as the argument, and which returns Self. The type of an instance of that class multiplied by 1.1 should be the timestamp class, but ty gives Unknown.
ty rejects a float for the float form of my generic "exactly this type" protocol (read and write class property of type[T]). Accept float, still reject int and bool.

ty no longer sees that the negative branch of the standard library check "is this object a dataclass" is unreachable for a concrete dataclass. Example: a dataclass with one int field, and a function whose parameter is annotated with that dataclass. Inside a branch where the check returns false for the parameter, ty reveals the dataclass intersected with the negation of the protocol that this check narrows to and the negation of the type of that protocol. The revealed type should be Never.

This worked before a recent change only by accident, through an earlier treatment of the return types of type-narrowing functions. That treatment should not have made a difference here, because that protocol is not generic.

The cause: a concrete dataclass is assignable to that protocol, but it is not a subtype of it. The protocol has a class-level member, the mapping of field names to field objects, whose type contains Any. ty gives dataclasses a member of the same type, but a type that contains Any is not a subtype of itself. A possible fix is to make that member non-gradual (for example a covariant mapping with object instead of Any), and possibly read-only.
For a value typed as a concrete dataclass, ty should narrow the negative branch of the standard is-it-a-dataclass check to Never. Now it keeps the dataclass type there.

ty fails to infer a precise type when a type variable sits inside a class-object parameter type. Example: a generic class with one type variable, and a subclass of it that fills the type variable with a sequence of strings. Another class has a method whose parameter is annotated as the class object of the generic class with the type variable, and which returns that type variable. A function takes an instance of that other class and calls the method with the subclass itself (the class, not an instance). The result should be a sequence of strings, but ty reveals Unknown. Because of that, a call of a method that does not exist on the result is not reported. The reporter thinks this may be similar to other inference problems, but distinct.
ty infers Unknown when I pass a subclass of a specialized generic class where a class object of that generic is expected. It should infer the type argument.

In a match statement over an enum, ty does not narrow the value to Never after all members are matched, when two things hold: the enum class overrides the class method that the enum machinery calls for a value that is not a member, and the matched value comes from a function call.

Example with ty 0.0.70: an enum has two members, a and b, and overrides that hook as a class method that returns member a. A variable assigned directly to member a is matched with a case for a, a case for b and a wildcard case. In the wildcard case, the typing assertion that a value can never occur passes. A second variable gets its value from a function annotated to return the enum, and is matched in the same way. There the assertion fails: ty still sees the enum without the two members, not Never.

The override seems to make ty think that a function that returns the enum can return other values. It cannot, because Python raises a type error when the hook returns something that is not a valid member. Expected: the match is exhaustive in both cases.
ty does not see a match over all enum members as exhaustive when the enum overrides the hook for unknown values and the value comes from a function. Please fix.
